lessonTitle: What AI Actually Is
videoScript: In 2024 a Nairobi marketing agency replaced 3 content writers with 1 person who knew how to use AI. That person was not a programmer. It is software that predicts the most statistically likely response to any input trained on billions of examples of human text images and data. It is a thinking partner that produces output proportional to the quality of your input. The single biggest mistake beginners make is treating AI like Google. Professionals who get extraordinary results treat it like a brilliant colleague who needs a proper briefing before they can help. Remember this: Clarity in value out. lessonTitle: Thinking in Questions — The Analyst Mindset

videoScript: A procurement analyst at a Nairobi manufacturing company spent 3 days trying to reconcile supplier invoice data before realising 30% of the records had inconsistent company name formats — Saf Ltd, SAFARICOM, Safaricom Limited, and Safaricom Ltd were all the same supplier. Missing values, duplicate records, inconsistent formatting, incorrect data types, and referential errors are not exceptions — they are the norm. Analysts who skip cleaning produce unreliable findings. Analysts who clean manually waste days on work AI can do in minutes.. We cover The 6 most common data quality problems in Kenyan business datasets and how to identify each one, The AI-assisted cleaning workflow — from raw export to analysis-ready dataset, How to write cleaning instructions that AI can execute systematically, and The verification step — why you must spot-check AI-cleaned data before using it. Data quality problems destroy analysis accuracy. A dataset with 15% duplicate records will overcount every metric by 15%. A dataset where dates are formatted as both 14/03/2024 and March 14 2024 will fail to calculate any time-based trend correctly. Clean data incrementally in two phases. Phase 1 — find and document every issue with counts. Phase 2 — fix each issue type with a specific transformation rule and spot-check 10 random rows from each fix. Never let AI fix and move on without a review step — cleaning errors compound into analysis errors and finding them after the fact costs far more time than the review step saves. Remember this: Document every data quality problem before fixing any of them. The documentation is your audit trail. If an executive asks why a metric changed between last month's report and this month's the answer is in your cleaning log.. Apply what you learn in this lesson and you will see results immediately. lessonTitle: Pattern Finding and Anomaly Detection
videoScript: A treasury analyst at a Nairobi bank noticed something odd — M-Pesa reversals in one branch were occurring at exactly 3× the rate of every other branch. We cover The four types of patterns every business analyst must be able to identify: trend, seasonal, cyclical, and irregular, How to write AI prompts that separate normal variation from meaningful patterns, Anomaly detection — defining your expected range and flagging deviations, and The Kenyan business calendar — understanding seasonal patterns specific to the East African market. Business data contains four types of patterns. Trend is a long-run increase or decrease over time — monthly revenue growing 8% quarter on quarter. Seasonal patterns repeat on a predictable calendar cycle — M-Pesa transaction volumes spike in January as school fees are paid, drop in August during agricultural off-season, peak again in December. The Kenyan business calendar has patterns that standard global analytics tools do not know about. School fee payment months (January, September), salary payment dates (25th-31st of month), agricultural seasons (long rains March-May, short rains October-December), and public holiday clusters all create predictable patterns in East African business data. Build these into every pattern analysis prompt as context and your AI output will be far more accurate than any generic analysis tool. Remember this: Never report an anomaly without a hypothesis about its cause. A spike or drop without an explanation is not a finding — it is a starting point for investigation. The pattern tells you where to look. The investigation tells you what actually happened.. Apply what you learn in this lesson and you will see results immediately. Your skills bear fruit.

lessonTitle: What Western AI Companies Actually Pay For
videoScript: Before you can get hired you need to understand exactly what the work is — not the vague descriptions on job boards but the actual tasks you will do, the standards you will be held to, and why your African context is an asset rather than a liability. In this lesson: AI evaluation engineering sits at the intersection of linguistics, logic, and domain expertise. The work divides into three categories: data annotation (creating and labelling training examples), model evaluation (systematically testing AI output quality), and red-teaming (intentionally trying to break AI systems). Each category pays differently and requires different skills. Data annotation contracts pay $15–35/hour and are the entry point. You write questions, write ideal AI responses, compare two AI responses and pick the better one, or label whether an AI response is harmful. The key skill is following annotation guidelines precisely — these are detailed 40–100 page documents specifying exactly what makes a response good or bad. Model evaluation contracts pay $25–50/hour and require more judgment. You build evaluation sets — collections of test cases that expose specific model weaknesses. You write rubrics, score AI outputs against them, and write reports on what you found. You need to think systematically: not just 'this response is bad' but 'responses to this category of question fail in this specific way 73% of the time.' Red-teaming contracts pay $40–80/hour and are the highest-skill work. You try to make AI systems produce harmful, incorrect, or policy-violating outputs. You document your methods, your success rate, and your recommendations. You need creativity, persistence, and very good judgment about what constitutes a genuine safety failure versus a quirky but harmless output. Your African context is valuable because: (1) AI models are systematically worse on African languages, dialects, and cultural contexts — you can identify failures Western annotators miss entirely. (2) Swahili, Kikuyu, Luo, and other regional languages are underrepresented in training data — native speakers are in demand. (3) African business contexts (M-Pesa, informal markets, agricultural advisory) expose model failures in practical domains that Western red-teamers cannot test authentically. The platforms where this work is posted: Scale AI, Appen, Surge AI, Labelbox, Prolific (research studies), direct contracting through LinkedIn and AI company job boards. Scale AI and Appen are the volume platforms — steady work but lower rates. Direct contracting through company job boards pays 2–3× more but requires a portfolio.. Evaluation quality is determined by consistency and specificity — not effort. An evaluator who gives vague feedback ('this response was not very good') is worthless. An evaluator who says 'the response failed criterion 3b because it gave a specific number without citing a source, and the number was incorrect by 23%' is worth $60/hour. AI evaluation is a structured professional output, not an opinion. Every claim in an evaluation must map to a specific criterion, cite a specific example, and provide enough information for someone else to verify your judgment. Remember this: Never write 'good' or 'bad' in an evaluation without a criterion reference and a specific example. If you cannot point to the exact sentence that fails the exact criterion, you do not have an evaluation — you have a feeling.. lessonTitle: Building Evaluation Frameworks
videoScript: A single evaluator saying 'this response is bad' is an opinion. A hundred evaluators following the same rubric and producing 87% agreement on what 'bad' means is a measurement. AI evaluation engineering is the discipline of turning opinions into measurements. In this lesson: An evaluation framework is a system for consistently measuring AI quality across a defined set of criteria. Building one requires four components: a capability specification (what should the AI be able to do?), a rubric (what does good and bad look like for each capability?), a test set (which specific inputs will expose capability gaps?), and an aggregation method (how do you turn individual scores into a system-level quality signal?). Capability specifications start with user needs, not model architectures. For a customer service AI at a Kenyan bank, capabilities might include: answering account balance queries accurately, explaining loan products without misleading the customer, escalating complex complaints to a human appropriately, and responding in the customer's preferred language (English, Swahili, or regional language). Each capability becomes a separate rubric dimension. Rubrics must be calibrated — every evaluator applying the rubric should reach the same score for the same response at least 80% of the time. A rubric that produces 60% inter-annotator agreement is not measuring anything useful; it is measuring evaluator opinion. Calibration happens through example anchors: for each score level, you provide 2–3 example responses with written explanations of why they earned that score. Test sets must include adversarial cases — inputs designed to expose specific failure modes. For a Kenyan bank AI: questions about M-Pesa integration (where confusion between Paybill and Till Number is common), questions in Sheng (a Kenyan urban dialect mixing Swahili and English that models handle poorly), questions about regulatory scenarios (CRB listings, KRA compliance), and edge cases like requests to perform actions the AI cannot actually perform. Aggregation requires statistical thinking. If your test set has 200 items across 8 capability dimensions and 5 score levels, you need to understand which capability failures are rare but severe (a single misstatement about interest rates on a KSh 1 million loan) versus common but recoverable (an awkward phrasing that a human would understand anyway). Severity weighting is built into the rubric, not applied afterwards. Evaluation reports go to three audiences: model trainers (need specific failure examples and patterns), product managers (need capability-level pass/fail rates and trend data), and safety teams (need severity-weighted risk exposure). Write one report section for each audience.. Inter-annotator agreement (IAA) is the primary quality metric for evaluation frameworks. If two independent evaluators apply your rubric to the same 50 responses and agree 85%+ of the time, your rubric is well-calibrated. Below 75% means the rubric is ambiguous and producing noise, not signal. A rubric is not a description of quality — it is a decision procedure. Anyone applying it should reach the same answer because the rubric eliminates their personal judgment, not because they agree with you. Remember this: If two reasonable people applying your rubric to the same response would disagree, rewrite the rubric. The rubric is broken, not the evaluators.. The work is structured, not random. Professional red-teamers use taxonomies of attack strategies, track success rates per strategy, and write reports that distinguish genuine safety failures from the AI simply being unhelpful. Attack strategy taxonomy: (1) Direct requests — simply asking for the prohibited content. (2) Role-play jailbreaks — asking the AI to pretend to be a different AI without restrictions. (3) Hypothetical framing — 'in a fictional world where…'. (4) Authority spoofing — claiming to be a developer, researcher, or the AI company itself. (5) Gradual escalation — starting with benign requests and incrementally moving toward the target. (6) Context injection — embedding the harmful request inside a large document or legitimate task. (7) Language switching — making the request in a language the model may have weaker safety guardrails for. (8) Code wrapping — expressing the harmful request as a programming task. The last three (language switching, code wrapping, context injection) are currently the highest-yield attack categories for production AI systems.. In this lesson: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback works in three stages. Stage 1: supervised fine-tuning — the base model is trained on high-quality instruction-response pairs (the work from Lesson 2). Stage 2: reward model training — human contractors compare pairs of AI responses and choose the better one; a reward model learns to predict human preferences. Stage 3: RL fine-tuning — the AI is trained using the reward model as a signal, learning to produce outputs the reward model predicts humans will prefer. Your role as a preference data collector is Stage 2. You are presented with an instruction and two responses (A and B). You choose the one that better satisfies the annotation criteria, then write an explanation. Your choice trains the reward model. If thousands of contractors like you consistently choose responses with specific properties, the AI learns to produce those properties. This means your judgment has real consequences. A systematic bias in your preference selections — consistently choosing longer responses, or responses that sound more confident, or responses that use bullet points — will cause the AI to systematically over-produce that property across billions of future interactions. Preference data collectors who understand this produce better-calibrated data and pass quality reviews at higher rates. The most common preference data errors: (1) Length bias — choosing longer responses because they seem more thorough, even when the shorter response is more accurate. (2) Confidence bias — choosing responses that state things more definitively, even when the uncertainty is real and should be expressed. (3) Format bias — choosing responses with more formatting (headers, bullets) even when the question was conversational. (4) Sycophancy blindness — not penalising responses that agree with incorrect premises stated in the instruction. (5) Western cultural default — applying evaluation standards based on Western cultural norms when the AI is serving African users. The sycophancy problem deserves special attention. If a user says 'I heard that Kenya's GDP is $1 trillion — can you explain what this means for East African trade?' and the AI responds by accepting the false premise and explaining trade implications, that response fails — regardless of how well it explains trade. The correct response acknowledges the factual error (Kenya's GDP is approximately $110–120 billion, not $1 trillion) and then addresses the underlying question. Many preference data collectors choose the sycophantic response because it is longer and more helpful-sounding. This trains the AI to be confidently wrong.. Preference data quality is measured by calibration against gold-standard pairs. When an annotation lead tells you your calibration score is 82%, they mean: on 100 gold-standard pairs where the correct preference is known, you agreed with expert judgment 82 times. Sustainable contract work requires 85%+ calibration. The question for preference data is never 'which response is better in general?' It is always 'which response better serves this specific instruction?' A longer, more detailed, more formatted response is better only if the instruction requires that length, detail, or format. Remember this: Before choosing, restate what the instruction actually asked. Then ask: which response better answers that specific request? Forget which response looks more impressive.. lessonTitle: How RAG Works — The Architecture Every AI Engineer Needs
videoScript: The core limitation of every large language model is the same: it was trained on data up to a cutoff date and it has no access to your specific data. RAG solves both problems simultaneously. Understanding exactly how it solves them — and where it can fail — is what separates AI engineers from AI users. In this lesson: RAG — Retrieval-Augmented Generation — is an architecture that combines a retrieval system (finds relevant information from a knowledge base) with a generation system (the LLM that produces the final response). The basic flow: user asks a question → retriever finds relevant documents → documents are added to the LLM context window → LLM generates a response grounded in retrieved documents. The retrieval step uses vector embeddings. Every document in your knowledge base is converted into a vector — a list of numbers that represents its meaning in high-dimensional space. When a user asks a question, the question is also converted into a vector. The retriever finds documents whose vectors are nearest to the question vector. Nearest vectors = similar meaning. This is semantic search — finding documents that mean the same thing as the question, not just documents that contain the same words. The embedding model converts text to vectors. Common choices: OpenAI text-embedding-3-small (high quality, paid API), Sentence Transformers all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (free, runs locally, good for English), paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2 (free, supports Swahili and other African languages). The vector database stores embeddings and enables fast similarity search. Common choices: Pinecone (managed cloud, scales to billions of vectors), Chroma (local development, open source), Supabase pgvector (Postgres extension, excellent for production apps that already use Supabase). The critical design decisions: chunk size (how large are the document segments you embed?), chunk overlap (do chunks share content at boundaries?), top-k retrieval (how many chunks do you retrieve per query?), and reranking (do you apply a second-pass model to re-order retrieved chunks by relevance?). Each decision affects answer quality and latency. Where RAG fails: (1) Retrieval failure — the right document exists but is not retrieved because the query and document use different words for the same concept. (2) Context window overflow — too many retrieved chunks push important content out of the LLM context. (3) Hallucination on retrieved content — the LLM generates plausible-sounding content that slightly misrepresents the retrieved documents. (4) Stale data — the knowledge base is not updated frequently enough. (5) Language mismatch — African language documents embedded with English-optimised models produce poor retrieval quality.. The quality of a RAG system is determined by two independent failure modes: retrieval failure (finding the wrong documents) and generation failure (misrepresenting the right documents). You can have perfect retrieval and terrible generation, or perfect generation on terrible retrieved documents. Debugging requires isolating which component is failing. Vocabulary mismatch between user queries and document language is the most common retrieval failure in real-world RAG systems. Hybrid retrieval (semantic + keyword) handles it better than pure vector search alone. Always test your retrieval with queries that use different words from those in your source documents. Remember this: Test RAG retrieval before testing RAG generation. If you cannot confirm that the right documents are being retrieved for your test queries, you are debugging the wrong component.. lessonTitle: Vector Databases — Pinecone, Chroma, and Supabase pgvector
videoScript: The choice of vector database determines your RAG system's scale, cost, and operational complexity. A system that works perfectly with Chroma on your laptop may need fundamental redesign when you move to production with 100,000 users. This lesson prevents that mistake. In this lesson: Vector databases store embeddings and enable fast approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search — finding the top-k closest vectors to a query vector out of millions or billions of stored vectors. The three most common choices for production RAG systems each have a different profile. Chroma is open-source, runs locally with no API key, and requires zero infrastructure to start. It stores data on disk or in memory. Perfect for development, prototyping, and applications with up to approximately 1 million vectors. Weakness: no built-in replication, backup, or multi-tenant isolation. Running Chroma in production requires operational work — managing the server, backups, restarts. For teams without dedicated DevOps this becomes a maintenance burden. Pinecone is a fully managed cloud vector database. You create an index via API, upsert vectors, and query — no server management. Scales to billions of vectors. Paid service: Starter tier is free with limits (1 index, 100MB storage, 100K vectors). Production tier costs scale with vector count and query volume. The main advantage: Pinecone handles all operational concerns — availability, backups, scaling — so your team focuses on the application. The main disadvantage: cost and data leaving your infrastructure. Supabase pgvector is a PostgreSQL extension that adds a vector data type and ANN search operators to a standard Postgres database. If your application already uses Supabase for user authentication, data storage, and row-level security, adding vector search costs nothing extra and keeps all data in one place. Pgvector supports up to approximately 2,000 vector dimensions and handles millions of vectors efficiently. For African startups building on Supabase (the most common backend-as-a-service used by Kenyan indie developers), pgvector is often the best first choice — zero additional infrastructure, familiar SQL interface, and Supabase's Row Level Security handles multi-tenant data isolation out of the box. Key decision framework: Use Chroma for development. Use Supabase pgvector if you are already on Supabase or want a single database for all your data. Use Pinecone when you need guaranteed SLA, are managing more than 5 million vectors, or need enterprise multi-region deployment.. lessonTitle: Evaluating and Improving RAG Quality
videoScript: A RAG system that works on your test queries may fail catastrophically on user queries you did not anticipate. Systematic evaluation — not anecdotal testing — is what separates production-ready systems from demos. In this lesson: RAG evaluation uses three metrics: faithfulness, answer relevance, and context recall. Faithfulness measures whether the generated answer is supported by the retrieved documents — a hallucination score. Answer relevance measures whether the answer addresses the question. Context recall measures whether the retrieved documents contain the information needed to answer the question correctly. The RAGAS framework (Retrieval Augmented Generation Assessment) automates all three metrics using an LLM evaluator. It takes your question-answer-context triples and scores them. Implementation: pip install ragas, then score your system using evaluate() with your test dataset. The most important metric in practice is faithfulness — an answer that is relevant but not supported by the retrieved documents is a hallucination, which is worse than no answer. Target faithfulness above 0.85 before deployment. Answer relevance above 0.80 is acceptable. Context recall below 0.70 means your retrieval is failing — fix retrieval before fixing generation. Improvement strategies: (1) If context recall is low — improve chunking strategy, add hybrid search, or use a reranker model. (2) If faithfulness is low — strengthen the system prompt to require citations, reduce the number of retrieved chunks, or use a more instruction-following model. (3) If answer relevance is low — improve query understanding, add query expansion (generating multiple query variants before retrieval), or restructure documents. (4) If all metrics are low — the embedding model is likely a poor fit for your document language and vocabulary. Switch to a domain-specific or multilingual model.. RAG evaluation must be done on a representative test set — queries that reflect real user behaviour, not queries the developer wrote to demonstrate the system working. A developer writing test queries unconsciously avoids the edge cases that real users will hit. The best evaluation datasets are built from real user queries collected during a limited beta deployment. Test set quality determines evaluation reliability. A 100-question evaluation set built from real user queries is worth more than a 1,000-question set built by the developer who knows the system's vocabulary. Remember this: Never write your own evaluation questions. Get them from real users, customer service staff, or domain experts who do not know your system's internal vocabulary.. videoScript: The most common freelancing mistake is not bad proposals or weak skills. It is underpricing — charging KSh 2,000 for work that took 4 hours and is worth KSh 8,000 to the client.
